claim: The centrosome is the major microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells.
source: The centrosome is the major microtubule organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: The centrosome consists of two centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM).
source: It consists of two centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM) (reviewed in Conduit et al., 2015; Paz and Luders, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Centrosome assembly depends on PCM binding to centrioles.
source: Centrosome assembly depends on PCM binding to centrioles, PCM self-association and dynein-mediated PCM transport
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract.

claim: Centrosome assembly depends on PCM self-association.
source: Centrosome assembly depends on PCM binding to centrioles, PCM self-association and dynein-mediated PCM transport
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract.

claim: Centrosome assembly depends on dynein-mediated PCM transport.
source: Centrosome assembly depends on PCM binding to centrioles, PCM self-association and dynein-mediated PCM transport

claim: When centrioles are lost due to PLK4 depletion or inhibition, dynein-based transport and self-clustering of PCM proteins are sufficient to form a single compact MTOC.
source: We showed that when centrioles are lost due to PLK4 depletion or inhibition, dynein-based transport and self-clustering of PCM proteins are sufficient to form a single compact MTOC, which generates a dense radial microtubule array.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A single compact MTOC formed after centriole loss generates a dense radial microtubule array.
source: We showed that when centrioles are lost due to PLK4 depletion or inhibition, dynein-based transport and self-clustering of PCM proteins are sufficient to form a single compact MTOC, which generates a dense radial microtubule array.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Interphase self-assembly of PCM components depends on γ-tubulin.
source: Interphase self-assembly of PCM components depends on γ-tubulin, pericentrin, CDK5RAP2 and ninein, but not NEDD1, CEP152, or CEP192.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from depletion experiments.

claim: Interphase self-assembly of PCM components depends on pericentrin.

claim: Interphase self-assembly of PCM components depends on ninein.

claim: Interphase self-assembly of PCM components does not depend on CEP152.

claim: Formation of a compact acentriolar MTOC is inhibited by AKAP450-dependent PCM recruitment to the Golgi.
source: Formation of a compact acentriolar MTOC is inhibited by AKAP450-dependent PCM recruitment to the Golgi or by randomly organized CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubules, which keep PCM mobile and prevent its coalescence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing different knockout cell lines.

claim: Formation of a compact acentriolar MTOC is inhibited by randomly organized CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubules.
source: Formation of a compact acentriolar MTOC is inhibited by AKAP450-dependent PCM recruitment to the Golgi or by randomly organized CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubules, which keep PCM mobile and prevent its coalescence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing different knockout cell lines.

claim: CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubules keep PCM mobile and prevent its coalescence.
source: Formation of a compact acentriolar MTOC is inhibited by AKAP450-dependent PCM recruitment to the Golgi or by randomly organized CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubules, which keep PCM mobile and prevent its coalescence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and live imaging.

claim: Linking of CAMSAP2 to a minus-end-directed motor leads to the formation of an MTOC.
source: Linking of CAMSAP2 to a minus-end-directed motor leads to the formation of an MTOC, but MTOC compaction requires cooperation with pericentrin-containing self-clustering PCM.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data using inducible heterodimerization.

claim: MTOC compaction requires cooperation with pericentrin-containing self-clustering PCM.
source: Linking of CAMSAP2 to a minus-end-directed motor leads to the formation of an MTOC, but MTOC compaction requires cooperation with pericentrin-containing self-clustering PCM.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing cells with and without pericentrin.

claim: Interphase PCM contains a set of components that can self-assemble into a compact structure and organize microtubules.
source: Our data reveal that interphase PCM contains a set of components that can self-assemble into a compact structure and organize microtubules, but PCM self-organization is sensitive to motor- and microtubule-based rearrangement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: PCM self-organization is sensitive to motor- and microtubule-based rearrangement.
source: Our data reveal that interphase PCM contains a set of components that can self-assemble into a compact structure and organize microtubules, but PCM self-organization is sensitive to motor- and microtubule-based rearrangement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy studies have shown that PCM has a distinct organization.
source: For a long time it was thought that the PCM is amorphous, but super-resolution microscopy studies have shown that it has a distinct organization, with some proteins likely attached to the centriole wall and others organized around them (Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2014; Mennella et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Some PCM proteins are likely attached to the centriole wall and others organized around them.
source: For a long time it was thought that the PCM is amorphous, but super-resolution microscopy studies have shown that it has a distinct organization, with some proteins likely attached to the centriole wall and others organized around them (Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2014; Mennella et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The distinct organization of PCM is more obvious in interphase than in mitosis.
source: This distinct organization is more obvious in interphase than in mitosis, when the microtubule-organizing capacity of the centrosome increases due to enhanced PCM recruitment.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact based on prior research.

claim: The microtubule-organizing capacity of the centrosome increases during mitosis due to enhanced PCM recruitment.
source: This distinct organization is more obvious in interphase than in mitosis, when the microtubule-organizing capacity of the centrosome increases due to enhanced PCM recruitment.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact based on prior research.

claim: Many PCM components are known to oligomerize and interact with each other.
source: Many PCM components are known to oligomerize and interact with each other, and recent work suggested that the phase separation of interacting PCM components might contribute to centrosome assembly during mitosis (Raff, 2019; Woodruff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Phase separation of interacting PCM components might contribute to centrosome assembly during mitosis.
source: Many PCM components are known to oligomerize and interact with each other, and recent work suggested that the phase separation of interacting PCM components might contribute to centrosome assembly during mitosis (Raff, 2019; Woodruff et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Various cell-type-specific assemblies of PCM components can form clusters that are able to nucleate and organize microtubules and serve as MTOCs in the absence of centrioles, particularly during the formation of mitotic spindle poles.
source: This idea is underscored by data showing that various cell-type-specific assemblies of PCM components can form clusters that are able to nucleate and organize microtubules and serve as MTOCs in the absence of centrioles, particularly during the formation of mitotic spindle poles (Balestra et al., 2021; Chinen et al., 2021; Gartenmann et al., 2020; Meitinger et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020; Yeow et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic dynein is a motor that can bind to different PCM proteins and transport them to the centrosome-anchored microtubule ends.
source: Furthermore, an important centrosome component, cytoplasmic dynein, is a motor that can bind to different PCM proteins and transport them to the centrosome-anchored microtubule ends, where these PCM proteins can nucleate and anchor additional microtubules, thus generating a positive feedback loop in centrosome assembly (Balczon et al., 1999; Burakov et al., 2008; Purohit et al., 1999; Redwine et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: PCM proteins transported by dynein to centrosome-anchored microtubule ends can nucleate and anchor additional microtubules, thus generating a positive feedback loop in centrosome assembly.
source: Furthermore, an important centrosome component, cytoplasmic dynein, is a motor that can bind to different PCM proteins and transport them to the centrosome-anchored microtubule ends, where these PCM proteins can nucleate and anchor additional microtubules, thus generating a positive feedback loop in centrosome assembly (Balczon et al., 1999; Burakov et al., 2008; Purohit et al., 1999; Redwine et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Dynein and its mitotic binding partner NuMA strongly participate in the formation of mitotic and meiotic spindle poles.
source: Dynein and its mitotic binding partner NuMA also strongly participate in the formation of mitotic and meiotic spindle poles (Chinen et al., 2020; Khodjakov et al., 2000; Kolano et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In most differentiated cell types, centrosome function is suppressed.
source: These properties, such as the ability of PCM to cluster or form molecular condensates, nucleate and anchor microtubules and move with motor proteins, are relevant because in most differentiated cell types, centrosome function is suppressed, and some PCM components form acentrosomal MTOCs (Muroyama and Lechler, 2017; Sallee and Feldman, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In most differentiated cell types, some PCM components form acentrosomal MTOCs.
source: These properties, such as the ability of PCM to cluster or form molecular condensates, nucleate and anchor microtubules and move with motor proteins, are relevant because in most differentiated cell types, centrosome function is suppressed, and some PCM components form acentrosomal MTOCs (Muroyama and Lechler, 2017; Sallee and Feldman, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: During mitotic exit, when mitotic kinases are inactivated, PCM complexes can be removed from the centrosomes as 'fragments' or 'packets'.
source: During mitotic exit, when mitotic kinases are inactivated, PCM complexes can be removed from the centrosomes as 'fragments' or 'packets' (Magescas et al., 2019; Rusan and Wadsworth, 2005), indicating that they maintain some degree of self-association.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: PCM complexes removed from centrosomes during mitotic exit maintain some degree of self-association.
source: During mitotic exit, when mitotic kinases are inactivated, PCM complexes can be removed from the centrosomes as 'fragments' or 'packets' (Magescas et al., 2019; Rusan and Wadsworth, 2005), indicating that they maintain some degree of self-association.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited observations.

claim: Centrioles were removed using the PLK4 kinase inhibitor centrinone B which blocks centriole duplication.
source: To study centriole-independent function and dynamics of PCM proteins, we removed centrioles using the PLK4 kinase inhibitor centrinone B which blocks centriole duplication (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation.

claim: In most commonly studied cultured cell lines, microtubule networks are dense, and the centrosome is not the only MTOC.
source: Importantly, in most commonly studied cultured cell lines, such as fibroblasts, epithelial, endothelial or cancer cells, microtubule networks are dense, and the centrosome is not the only MTOC.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cell biology.

claim: In commonly studied cultured cell lines, non-centrosomal microtubule minus ends are often stabilized by the members of CAMSAP family.
source: In such cells, non-centrosomal microtubule minus ends are often stabilized by the members of CAMSAP family (Jiang et al., 2014; Meng et al., 2008; Tanaka et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The Golgi apparatus serves as a second MTOC which nucleates and anchors a very significant proportion of microtubules.
source: and the Golgi apparatus serves as a second MTOC which nucleates and anchors a very significant proportion of microtubules (Efimov et al., 2007; Rios, 2014; Wu et al., 2016; Zhu and Kaverina, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: If centrosomes are lost because centriole duplication is blocked by inhibiting PLK4 or depleting another essential centriole component, Golgi-dependent microtubule organization becomes predominant.
source: If centrosomes are lost because centriole duplication is blocked by inhibiting PLK4 or depleting another essential centriole component, Golgi-dependent microtubule organization becomes predominant (Gavilan et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The ability of the Golgi complex to serve as an MTOC critically depends on the Golgi adaptor AKAP450.
source: The ability of the Golgi complex to serve as an MTOC critically depends on the Golgi adaptor AKAP450, which recruits several PCM components that nucleate microtubules including the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), CDK5RAP2 and pericentrin (Gavilan et al., 2018; Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: AKAP450 recruits several PCM components that nucleate microtubules including the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), CDK5RAP2 and pericentrin.
source: The ability of the Golgi complex to serve as an MTOC critically depends on the Golgi adaptor AKAP450, which recruits several PCM components that nucleate microtubules including the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), CDK5RAP2 and pericentrin (Gavilan et al., 2018; Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: AKAP450 tethers microtubule minus ends stabilized by CAMSAP2 to the Golgi membranes.
source: Moreover, AKAP450 also tethers microtubule minus ends stabilized by CAMSAP2 to the Golgi membranes (Gavilan et al., 2018; Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In the absence of AKAP450, the Golgi ribbon is maintained.
source: In the absence of AKAP450, the Golgi ribbon is maintained, but neither PCM components nor CAMSAP-stabilized microtubule minus ends can be attached to the Golgi membranes and they are instead dispersed in cytoplasm, leading to a randomly organized microtubule network (Gavilan et al., 2018; Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In the absence of AKAP450, neither PCM components nor CAMSAP-stabilized microtubule minus ends can be attached to the Golgi membranes and they are instead dispersed in cytoplasm.
source: In the absence of AKAP450, the Golgi ribbon is maintained, but neither PCM components nor CAMSAP-stabilized microtubule minus ends can be attached to the Golgi membranes and they are instead dispersed in cytoplasm, leading to a randomly organized microtubule network (Gavilan et al., 2018; Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In the absence of AKAP450, dispersal of PCM components and CAMSAP-stabilized microtubule minus ends leads to a randomly organized microtubule network.
source: In the absence of AKAP450, the Golgi ribbon is maintained, but neither PCM components nor CAMSAP-stabilized microtubule minus ends can be attached to the Golgi membranes and they are instead dispersed in cytoplasm, leading to a randomly organized microtubule network (Gavilan et al., 2018; Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A single compact acentriolar MTOC (caMTOC) can form after centriole loss in AKAP450 knockout cells, if the stabilization of free minus ends in these cells is disabled by knocking out CAMSAP2.
source: However, this notion appears to be inaccurate: in our previous study in RPE1 cells, we observed that a single compact acentriolar MTOC (caMTOC) can still form after centriole loss in AKAP450 knockout cells, if the stabilization of free minus ends in these cells is disabled by knocking out CAMSAP2 (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: RPE1 cells were treated for 11 days with the PLK4 inhibitor centrinone B to induce centriole loss.
source: To study centriole-independent PCM organization and dynamics in interphase cells, we induced centriole loss in RPE1 cells by treating them for 11 days with the PLK4 inhibitor centrinone B (Wong et al., 2015; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: In wild type cells treated with centrinone B, PCM relocalized to the Golgi apparatus.
source: In wild type (WT) cells, PCM (detected with antibodies against pericentrin) relocalized to the Golgi apparatus, and the microtubule array reorganized around the Golgi membranes, as described previously (Gavilan et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D and citations to previous studies.

claim: In wild type cells treated with centrinone B, the microtubule array reorganized around the Golgi membranes.
source: In wild type (WT) cells, PCM (detected with antibodies against pericentrin) relocalized to the Golgi apparatus, and the microtubule array reorganized around the Golgi membranes, as described previously (Gavilan et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D and citations to previous studies.

claim: In AKAP450 knockout cells treated with centrinone B, centriole loss led to the appearance of strongly dispersed PCM clusters.
source: In AKAP450 knockout cells, centriole loss led to the appearance of strongly dispersed PCM clusters, which could no longer bind to the Golgi, and a highly disorganized microtubule system, consistent with published work (Gavilan et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E and citations to previous studies.

claim: In AKAP450 knockout cells treated with centrinone B, dispersed PCM clusters could no longer bind to the Golgi.
source: In AKAP450 knockout cells, centriole loss led to the appearance of strongly dispersed PCM clusters, which could no longer bind to the Golgi, and a highly disorganized microtubule system, consistent with published work (Gavilan et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E and citations to previous studies.

claim: In AKAP450 knockout cells treated with centrinone B, a highly disorganized microtubule system was observed.
source: In AKAP450 knockout cells, centriole loss led to the appearance of strongly dispersed PCM clusters, which could no longer bind to the Golgi, and a highly disorganized microtubule system, consistent with published work (Gavilan et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E and citations to previous studies.

claim: In AKAP450/CAMSAP2 double knockout cells treated with centrinone B, a single caMTOC with microtubules focused around it was observed.
source: In contrast, in AKAP450/CAMSAP2 double knockout cells, a single caMTOC with microtubules focused around it was observed (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Formation of a single caMTOC was also observed in AKAP450 knockout cells transiently depleted of CAMSAP2 by siRNA transfection.
source: Formation of a single caMTOC was also observed in AKAP450 knockout cells transiently depleted of CAMSAP2 by siRNA transfection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Brefeldin A disrupts the Golgi.
source: As an alternative approach to block the ability of the Golgi apparatus to recruit PCM, we treated the cells with Brefeldin A, which disrupts the Golgi (Klausner et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Brefeldin A by itself had no effect on centrosome integrity but led to the dispersal of the Golgi marker GM130.
source: As expected, Brefeldin A by itself had no effect on centrosome integrity but led to the dispersal of the Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: In centrinone-treated wild-type cells, PCM was dispersed after Golgi disruption with Brefeldin A.
source: In centrinone-treated wild-type cells, PCM was dispersed after Golgi disruption, and the same was true for the majority of CAMSAP2 knockout cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: In 12% of CAMSAP2 knockout cells treated with both centrinone B and Brefeldin A, PCM compaction was observed.
source: However, in 12% of CAMSAP2 knockout cells treated with both centrinone B and Brefeldin A, we observed PCM compaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F), similar to that seen in AKAP450/CAMSAP2 double knockout cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Unlike centrosomes, which always have a spherical shape, caMTOCs in AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells were cylindrical in ~35% of the cells.
source: Unlike centrosomes, which always have a spherical shape, caMTOCs in AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells were cylindrical in ~35% of the cells, whereas in the remaining cells that lacked centrioles based on staining for centrin, MTOCs had a round shape (~38% of the cells); the rest of the centrin-negative cells either had dispersed PCM clusters (~7%) or no detectable PCM clusters (~11%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: In ~38% of centrin-negative AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells, MTOCs had a round shape.
source: Unlike centrosomes, which always have a spherical shape, caMTOCs in AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells were cylindrical in ~35% of the cells, whereas in the remaining cells that lacked centrioles based on staining for centrin, MTOCs had a round shape (~38% of the cells); the rest of the centrin-negative cells either had dispersed PCM clusters (~7%) or no detectable PCM clusters (~11%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: ~72% of acentriolar AKAP450 knockout cells had dispersed PCM.
source: In contrast,~72% of acentriolar AKAP450 knockout cells had dispersed PCM, while caMTOCs were very rare (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Cylindrical caMTOCs in AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells consisted of small clusters of PCM components, including pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin, ninein and dynein heavy chain.
source: Analysis by Stimulated Emission Depletion (STED) microscopy revealed that cylindrical caMTOCs in AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells consisted of small clusters of PCM components, including pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin, ninein and dynein heavy chain (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F using STED microscopy.

claim: caMTOCs with a clearly elongated shape had an average length of ~11 µm and an average width of ~1.5 µm.
source: caMTOCs with a clearly elongated shape had an average length of ~11 µm and an average width of ~1.5 µm (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells, GFP-CDK5RAP2 was strongly enriched within caMTOCs.
source: In centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells, it was strongly enriched within caMTOCs and sometimes also present in small motile clusters around a caMTOC (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: When the whole caMTOC was bleached in FRAP assays, the recovery was very slow and incomplete.
source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) assays showed that when the whole caMTOC was bleached, the recovery was very slow and incomplete (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H, I.

claim: Highly condensed caMTOCs displayed a slow redistribution of GFP-CDK5RAP2 signal, suggesting that their components are largely immobile and do not rearrange.
source: Highly condensed caMTOCs displayed a slow redistribution of GFP-CDK5RAP2 signal, suggesting that their components are largely immobile and do not rearrange.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRAP data.

claim: In more loosely organized caMTOCs, some rearrangement of small PCM clusters was observed.
source: In more loosely organized caMTOCs, some rearrangement of small PCM clusters was observed (Figure 1H, I); however, the recovery was still far from complete.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H, I.

claim: caMTOCs display variable degrees of compaction.
source: These data indicate that caMTOCs display variable degrees of compaction and are composed of PCM clusters that display limited exchange of GFP-CDK5RAP2 with the cytoplasmic pool, possibly because most of the GFP-CDK5RAP2 is accumulated within the caMTOC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP data.

claim: caMTOCs are composed of PCM clusters that display limited exchange of GFP-CDK5RAP2 with the cytoplasmic pool.
source: These data indicate that caMTOCs display variable degrees of compaction and are composed of PCM clusters that display limited exchange of GFP-CDK5RAP2 with the cytoplasmic pool, possibly because most of the GFP-CDK5RAP2 is accumulated within the caMTOC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP data.

claim: Depletion of PLK4 using siRNAs caused the appearance of round or cylindrical caMTOCs, similar to those observed after PLK4 inhibition with centrinone B.
source: Depletion of PLK4 using siRNAs caused the appearance of round or cylindrical caMTOCs, similar to those observed after PLK4 inhibition with centrinone B, indicating that catalytically inactive PLK4 had no scaffolding role within these structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-F.

claim: Catalytically inactive PLK4 had no scaffolding role within caMTOCs.
source: Depletion of PLK4 using siRNAs caused the appearance of round or cylindrical caMTOCs, similar to those observed after PLK4 inhibition with centrinone B, indicating that catalytically inactive PLK4 had no scaffolding role within these structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of PLK4 depletion and inhibition experiments.

claim: The percentage of cells with caMTOCs increased over time after PLK4 depletion.
source: The percentage of cells with caMTOCs increased over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), possibly due to the gradual depletion of PLK4.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Depletion of CPAP led to centriole loss but was much less efficient in inducing caMTOCs than PLK4 depletion.
source: In contrast, depletion of CPAP, an essential centriole biogenesis factor (Kohlmaier et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009), which also led to centriole loss, was much less efficient in inducing caMTOCs, and cylindrical caMTOCs were never observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E and citations.

claim: After CPAP depletion, cells in which pericentrin formed dispersed clusters or no visible clusters predominated (~67%).
source: After CPAP depletion, cells in which pericentrin formed dispersed clusters or no visible clusters predominated (~67%, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: Treatment of CPAP-depleted AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells with centrinone B for 1 day promoted the assembly of round or cylindrical caMTOCs.
source: Treatment of CPAP-depleted AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells with centrinone B for 1 day promoted the assembly of round or cylindrical caMTOCs, and the proportion of such cells increased to ~55% after 3 days of centrinone B treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-G.

claim: The inhibition of PLK1 with BI2536 has no effect on the formation of caMTOCs.
source: We also tested whether the inhibition of PLK1, a kinase that is known to be a major regulator of PCM self-assembly in mitosis (Haren et al., 2009; Joukov et al., 2014; Lee and Rhee, 2011), has an effect on the formation of caMTOCs by treating cells with BI2536 (a highly selective and potent inhibitor of PLK1), but found this not to be the case (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D and citations.

claim: The abundant PCM components pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, ninein and γ-tubulin colocalized within caMTOCs.
source: As indicated above, the abundant PCM components pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, ninein and γ-tubulin colocalized within caMTOCs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Three major PCM proteins, CEP152, CEP192 and NEDD1, could not be detected in caMTOCs although they were present in centrosomes of AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout RPE1 cells that were not treated with centrinone B.
source: In contrast, three other major PCM proteins, CEP152, CEP192 and NEDD1, could not be detected in these structures although they were present in centrosomes of AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout RPE1 cells that were not treated with centrinone B (Figure 2A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: CEP152, CEP192 and NEDD1 were expressed in centrinone-treated cells.
source: In contrast, three other major PCM proteins, CEP152, CEP192 and NEDD1, could not be detected in these structures although they were present in centrosomes of AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout RPE1 cells that were not treated with centrinone B (Figure 2A–C) and were also expressed in centrinone-treated cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After the depletion of pericentrin, no clusters of other PCM components could be detected.
source: After the depletion of pericentrin, no clusters of other PCM components could be detected (Figure 2D, J and K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, J and K, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin quadruple knockout cells were unable to form a single caMTOC when treated with centrinone B.
source: However, we were able to knock out pericentrin in cells lacking AKAP450, CAMSAP2 and p53 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming that the loss of p53 makes the cells more tolerant to centrosome absence and allows them to divide even in the presence of centrinone B (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Video 1). Similar to pericentrin-depleted cells, these quadruple knockout cells were unable to form a single caMTOC when treated with centrinone B (Figure 2E and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: In acentriolar quadruple knockout cells (AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin), CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and cytoplasmic dynein displayed no clustering.
source: In these acentriolar quadruple knockout cells, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and cytoplasmic dynein displayed no clustering, while ninein and PCM1, a centriolar satellite protein that localizes closely around the centrosome in normal cells (Prosser and Pelletier, 2020), formed small clusters distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and a citation.

claim: In acentriolar quadruple knockout cells (AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin), ninein and PCM1 formed small clusters distributed throughout the cytoplasm.
source: In these acentriolar quadruple knockout cells, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and cytoplasmic dynein displayed no clustering, while ninein and PCM1, a centriolar satellite protein that localizes closely around the centrosome in normal cells (Prosser and Pelletier, 2020), formed small clusters distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and a citation.

claim: Loss of pericentrin had no effect on the expression of CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and ninein.
source: Loss of pericentrin had no effect on the expression of CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and ninein (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), indicating that clustering by pericentrin affects the organization but not the stability of these PCM components.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Clustering by pericentrin affects the organization but not the stability of CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and ninein.
source: Loss of pericentrin had no effect on the expression of CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and ninein (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), indicating that clustering by pericentrin affects the organization but not the stability of these PCM components.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the expression data.

claim: The depletion of CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin or ninein in centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells did not prevent the formation of small pericentrin clusters, but these failed to coalesce into a single caMTOC.
source: The depletion of CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin or ninein in centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells did not prevent the formation of small pericentrin clusters, but these failed to coalesce into a single caMTOC (Figure 2F–H and J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-H and J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The depletion of CEP152, CEP192, or NEDD1 had no effect on the formation of caMTOCs.
source: In contrast, the depletion of CEP152, CEP192, or NEDD1 had no effect on the formation of caMTOCs (Figure 2A–C and J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C and J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: caMTOCs contained several centriole biogenesis factors, including CPAP, CP110, and CEP120, but lacked centrin and CEP135.
source: caMTOCs contained several centriole biogenesis factors, including CPAP, CP110, and CEP120, but lacked centrin and CEP135; however, the depletion of different centriolar proteins did not affect caMTOC formation (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The depletion of different centriolar proteins did not affect caMTOC formation.
source: caMTOCs contained several centriole biogenesis factors, including CPAP, CP110, and CEP120, but lacked centrin and CEP135; however, the depletion of different centriolar proteins did not affect caMTOC formation (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Within caMTOCs, several proteins were detected including a component of the HAUS complex (HAUS2), the centrosomal protein CEP170, dynein, dynactin, CLASP1/2, CLIP-115, CLIP-170, chTOG, KIF2A, and KIF1C.
source: Within caMTOCs, we also detected a component of the HAUS complex (HAUS2), the centrosomal protein CEP170, dynein, dynactin, CLASP1/2, CLIP-115, CLIP-170, chTOG, KIF2A, and KIF1C (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Among the tested proteins, only cytoplasmic dynein appeared essential for caMTOC formation.
source: We tested the importance of some of these proteins for caMTOC formation by siRNA-mediated depletion (see Figure 2K for an overview), but among the tested proteins, only cytoplasmic dynein appeared essential for this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the depletion experiments.

claim: In dynein-depleted cells, no clusters of pericentrin or other PCM components could be detected after centrinone B treatment.
source: In dynein-depleted cells, no clusters of pericentrin or other PCM components could be detected after centrinone B treatment (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: EB1 and EB3 were not enriched within the caMTOCs.
source: Because we detected several microtubule plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs) in the caMTOCs, such as CLIP-170, CLASP1/2 and the large subunit of dynactin, p150Glued, we also tested for the presence of the core components of the +TIP machinery, EB1 and EB3, but found that they were not enriched within the caMTOCs (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: caMTOCs could still form in cells lacking EB3, CAMSAP2, the C-terminal partner-binding half of EB1, and AKAP450.
source: Using the previously described cells that lack EB3, CAMSAP2 and the C-terminal partner-binding half of EB1 (Yang et al., 2017), we generated a knockout cell line that also lacks AKAP450 and found that caMTOCs could still form in these cells (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 5B, C, and a citation.

claim: caMTOCs strongly affected the organization and density of the microtubule network in acentriolar cells.
source: Despite containing only a subset of centrosomal proteins, caMTOCs strongly affected the organization and density of the microtubule network in acentriolar cells: microtubules were focused around caMTOCs if present and disorganized in cells lacking caMTOCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Microtubules were focused around caMTOCs if present and disorganized in cells lacking caMTOCs.
source: Despite containing only a subset of centrosomal proteins, caMTOCs strongly affected the organization and density of the microtubule network in acentriolar cells: microtubules were focused around caMTOCs if present and disorganized in cells lacking caMTOCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The strongest loss of microtubule density was observed in cells lacking pericentrin, dynein or γ-tubulin.
source: The strongest loss of microtubule density was observed in cells lacking pericentrin, dynein or γ-tubulin, while milder phenotypes were observed in cells lacking CDK5RAP2 or ninein (Figure 3A, B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B and E.

claim: Milder phenotypes of microtubule density loss were observed in cells lacking CDK5RAP2 or ninein.
source: The strongest loss of microtubule density was observed in cells lacking pericentrin, dynein or γ-tubulin, while milder phenotypes were observed in cells lacking CDK5RAP2 or ninein (Figure 3A, B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B and E.

claim: Control cells (AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells treated with centrinone B and control siRNA) formed radial microtubule networks with ~12% non-radial microtubules.
source: Whereas control cells (AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells treated with centrinone B and control siRNA) formed radial microtubule networks with ~12% non-radial microtubules, acentriolar cells lacking pericentrin or cytoplasmic dynein had ~46% non-radial microtubules, and the depletion of CDK5RAP2, ninein and γ-tubulin led to an intermediate phenotype with 25–30% non-radial microtubules (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D and E.

claim: Acentriolar cells lacking pericentrin or cytoplasmic dynein had ~46% non-radial microtubules.
source: Whereas control cells (AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells treated with centrinone B and control siRNA) formed radial microtubule networks with ~12% non-radial microtubules, acentriolar cells lacking pericentrin or cytoplasmic dynein had ~46% non-radial microtubules, and the depletion of CDK5RAP2, ninein and γ-tubulin led to an intermediate phenotype with 25–30% non-radial microtubules (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D and E.

claim: The depletion of CDK5RAP2, ninein and γ-tubulin led to an intermediate phenotype with 25–30% non-radial microtubules.
source: Whereas control cells (AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout cells treated with centrinone B and control siRNA) formed radial microtubule networks with ~12% non-radial microtubules, acentriolar cells lacking pericentrin or cytoplasmic dynein had ~46% non-radial microtubules, and the depletion of CDK5RAP2, ninein and γ-tubulin led to an intermediate phenotype with 25–30% non-radial microtubules (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D and E.

claim: An acentriolar PCM assembly containing pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, ninein, γ-tubulin and dynein is sufficient to form a radial microtubule array, similar to a centrosome.
source: An acentriolar PCM assembly containing pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, ninein, γ-tubulin and dynein is thus sufficient to form a radial microtubule array, similar to a centrosome, and PCM clustering promotes dense microtubule organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: PCM clustering promotes dense microtubule organization.
source: An acentriolar PCM assembly containing pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, ninein, γ-tubulin and dynein is thus sufficient to form a radial microtubule array, similar to a centrosome, and PCM clustering promotes dense microtubule organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: caMTOCs fragmented into small clusters upon nocodazole treatment at 37 °C.
source: To test whether the formation and maintenance of caMTOCs depends on microtubules, we depolymerized them by treating cells with nocodazole at 37 °C and found that caMTOCs fragmented into small clusters upon nocodazole treatment and reassembled into a single structure after nocodazole washout (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: caMTOCs reassembled into a single structure after nocodazole washout.
source: To test whether the formation and maintenance of caMTOCs depends on microtubules, we depolymerized them by treating cells with nocodazole at 37 °C and found that caMTOCs fragmented into small clusters upon nocodazole treatment and reassembled into a single structure after nocodazole washout (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Treatment with dynapyrazole A for 3 hr had no effect on dynein expression.
source: We confirmed that treatment with dynapyrazole A for 3 hr had no effect on dynein expression (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The addition of dynapyrazole A before nocodazole treatment prevented the disassembly of caMTOCs.
source: and found that the addition of this drug before nocodazole treatment prevented the disassembly of caMTOCs, whereas the treatment of cells with dynapyrazole A during nocodazole washout strongly inhibited caMTOC re-assembly (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The treatment of cells with dynapyrazole A during nocodazole washout strongly inhibited caMTOC re-assembly.
source: and found that the addition of this drug before nocodazole treatment prevented the disassembly of caMTOCs, whereas the treatment of cells with dynapyrazole A during nocodazole washout strongly inhibited caMTOC re-assembly (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Both microtubule-dependent dispersal and coalescence of PCM clusters into caMTOCs are driven by dynein activity.
source: These data indicate that both microtubule-dependent dispersal and coalescence of PCM clusters into caMTOCs are driven by dynein activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dynapyrazole A experiments.

claim: After a few minutes of nocodazole treatment, when the microtubule density was significantly reduced, small PCM clusters started to move out of the caMTOC and undergo rapid directional motility with speeds of up to 2 µm/s.
source: After a few minutes of nocodazole treatment, when the microtubule density was significantly reduced, small PCM clusters started to move out of the caMTOC and undergo rapid directional motility with speeds of up to 2 µm/s, which is within the range characteristic for cytoplasmic dynein (Schlager et al., 2014; Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and a citation.

claim: Once microtubules were completely disassembled, the movement of GFP-CDK5RAP2-positive clusters stopped.
source: Once microtubules were completely disassembled, the movement of GFP-CDK5RAP2-positive clusters stopped, indicating that it is microtubule-dependent but occurs only when the microtubule network is partially depolymerized.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from live imaging.

claim: The movement of GFP-CDK5RAP2-positive clusters is microtubule-dependent but occurs only when the microtubule network is partially depolymerized.
source: Once microtubules were completely disassembled, the movement of GFP-CDK5RAP2-positive clusters stopped, indicating that it is microtubule-dependent but occurs only when the microtubule network is partially depolymerized.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the live imaging data.

claim: During microtubule disassembly by nocodazole at 37 °C, there is a transient stage when PCM clusters interact with only a few microtubules, some of which have their minus-ends facing outwards.
source: Since cluster dispersal toward the cell periphery could be blocked by a dynein inhibitor, and since cytoplasmic dynein is a minus-end-directed motor, these data indicate that during microtubule disassembly by nocodazole at 37 °C, there is a transient stage when PCM clusters interact with only a few microtubules, some of which have their minus-ends facing outwards, and these microtubules serve as tracks for PCM transport.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The cells contained a significant number of minus-end-out microtubules, and their proportion increased during early stages of nocodazole treatment.
source: We found that the cells contained a significant number of minus-end-out microtubules, and their proportion increased during early stages of nocodazole treatment, possibly because minus-end-out microtubules are more stable (Figure 4G, for example, minus-end-out microtubules constituted ~23% of the total microtubule length determined from kinesin-1 trajectories in the untreated cell and ~46% in the nocodazole-treated cell).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from motor-PAINT shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Minus-end-out microtubules could serve as tracks for outward movement of PCM, causing the disassembly of caMTOC when the overall microtubule density around the caMTOC was strongly reduced.
source: These microtubules could serve as tracks for outward movement of PCM, causing the disassembly of caMTOC when the overall microtubule density around the caMTOC was strongly reduced (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motor-PAINT data.

claim: The dense network of PCM-anchored microtubule minus-ends around a caMTOC allows for its compaction via dynein-mediated forces.
source: These data suggest that the dense network of PCM-anchored microtubule minus-ends around a caMTOC allows for its compaction via dynein-mediated forces, but that dynein can pull the caMTOC apart when microtubules are disorganized.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Dynein can pull the caMTOC apart when microtubules are disorganized.
source: These data suggest that the dense network of PCM-anchored microtubule minus-ends around a caMTOC allows for its compaction via dynein-mediated forces, but that dynein can pull the caMTOC apart when microtubules are disorganized.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: When all microtubules were depolymerized by a combination of cold (4 °C) and nocodazole treatment, caMTOCs did not fall apart.
source: To further confirm that caMTOC disassembly is an active microtubule-dependent process, we also depolymerized microtubules by a combination of cold (4 °C) and nocodazole treatment. When all microtubules were depolymerized, caMTOCs did not fall apart, even when the cells were subsequently warmed to 37 °C in the presence of nocodazole, so that microtubules could not re-grow (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: In cold (4 °C) treatment conditions, the continuity and cylindrical organization of the PCM cluster were often perturbed.
source: However, we noticed that in these conditions, the continuity and cylindrical organization of the PCM cluster were often perturbed.
evidence: This is an observation from the cold treatment experiments.

claim: The elongated arrangement of PCM components within caMTOCs is microtubule-driven.
source: This raised the possibility that the elongated arrangement of PCM components within caMTOCs is microtubule-driven.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that cold treatment perturbs cylindrical organization.

claim: When cells were subjected to cold (4 °C) treatment in the absence of nocodazole, most of microtubules depolymerized, but some short cold-stable microtubules remained associated with the caMTOC.
source: Indeed, when cells were subjected to cold (4 °C) treatment in the absence of nocodazole, most of microtubules depolymerized, but some short cold-stable microtubules remained associated with the caMTOC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PCM self-assembly in the absence of centrioles is microtubule-dependent.
source: These data indicate that PCM self-assembly in the absence of centrioles is microtubule-dependent, and microtubules are involved in shaping the PCM cluster.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Microtubules are involved in shaping the PCM cluster.
source: These data indicate that PCM self-assembly in the absence of centrioles is microtubule-dependent, and microtubules are involved in shaping the PCM cluster.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Once assembled, the PCM cluster is quite stable, unless microtubule organization is altered and dynein-driven microtubule-based transport pulls it apart.
source: Once assembled, the PCM cluster is quite stable, unless microtubule organization is altered and dynein-driven microtubule-based transport pulls it apart.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: When nocodazole-mediated microtubule disassembly was carried out at 4 °C, the caMTOC remained intact and after nocodazole washout it served as the major microtubule nucleation site.
source: When nocodazole-mediated microtubule disassembly was carried out at 4 °C, the caMTOC remained intact and after nocodazole washout it served as the major microtubule nucleation site, similar to the centrosome in untreated wild-type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Small PCM clusters positive for pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and the centriolar satellite protein PCM1 that co-localized with the plus-ends of microtubules could be detected 30 s after nocodazole washout.
source: Small PCM clusters positive for pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and the centriolar satellite protein PCM1 that co-localized with the plus-ends of microtubules (labeled with EB1) could be detected 30 s after nocodazole washout; these PCM clusters and nascent microtubules did not colocalize with the Golgi membranes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PCM clusters and nascent microtubules did not colocalize with the Golgi membranes 30 s after nocodazole washout.
source: Small PCM clusters positive for pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin and the centriolar satellite protein PCM1 that co-localized with the plus-ends of microtubules (labeled with EB1) could be detected 30 s after nocodazole washout; these PCM clusters and nascent microtubules did not colocalize with the Golgi membranes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ninein was not detected within the clusters at 30 s after nocodazole washout but could be found 2 min after nocodazole washout.
source: Ninein was not detected within the clusters at this early stage of microtubule regrowth but could be found 2 min after nocodazole washout.
evidence: This is an observation from the microtubule regrowth experiments.

claim: No clusters of CEP192 or NEDD1 were observed even 10 min after nocodazole washout.
source: In contrast, no clusters of CEP192 or NEDD1 were observed even 10 min after nocodazole washout (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The depletion of pericentrin, CDK5RAP2 and γ-tubulin strongly inhibited microtubule nucleation after nocodazole washout.
source: The depletion of pericentrin, CDK5RAP2 and γ-tubulin strongly inhibited microtubule nucleation in these conditions, whereas the depletion of dynein heavy chain or ninein had a milder effect (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The depletion of dynein heavy chain or ninein had a milder effect on microtubule nucleation after nocodazole washout.
source: The depletion of pericentrin, CDK5RAP2 and γ-tubulin strongly inhibited microtubule nucleation in these conditions, whereas the depletion of dynein heavy chain or ninein had a milder effect (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: CDK5RAP2 clusters with attached microtubules coalesced by undergoing microtubule-based movements.
source: Live cell imaging with GFP-CDK5RAP2 and SiR-tubulin showed that CDK5RAP2 clusters with attached microtubules coalesced by undergoing microtubule-based movements (Figure 5D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live cell imaging shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A partly radial microtubule system emerged already 2 min after nocodazole washout.
source: and measurements in cells fixed at different time points after nocodazole washout showed that a partly radial microtubule system emerged already 2 min after nocodazole washout (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Reassembly of a single caMTOC in the central part of the cell occurred within ~15 min after nocodazole washout.
source: Reassembly of a single caMTOC in the central part of the cell occurred within ~15 min after nocodazole washout, though it was less compact than in cells that were not treated with nocodazole (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-G.

claim: Depletion of pericentrin, γ-tubulin and dynein heavy chain strongly inhibited the reformation of a radial microtubule network during nocodazole washout.
source: Depletion of pericentrin, γ-tubulin and dynein heavy chain strongly inhibited the reformation of a radial microtubule network during nocodazole washout, whereas the effect of depleting CDK5RAP2 and ninein was less strong (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: The effect of depleting CDK5RAP2 and ninein on the reformation of a radial microtubule network during nocodazole washout was less strong than that of depleting pericentrin, γ-tubulin and dynein heavy chain.
source: Depletion of pericentrin, γ-tubulin and dynein heavy chain strongly inhibited the reformation of a radial microtubule network during nocodazole washout, whereas the effect of depleting CDK5RAP2 and ninein was less strong (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: When pericentrin was depleted, CDK5RAP2 clusters were not detectable, and the microtubule network, both before nocodazole treatment and after nocodazole washout, was disorganized.
source: Live cell imaging of acentriolar AKAP450/CAMSAP2 knockout RPE1 cells stably expressing GFP-CDK5RAP2 showed that when pericentrin was depleted, CDK5RAP2 clusters were not detectable, and the microtubule network, both before nocodazole treatment and after nocodazole washout, was disorganized (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 3.

claim: Pericentrin and γ-tubulin form microtubule-nucleating and anchoring units.
source: Taken together, our data show that pericentrin and γ-tubulin form microtubule-nucleating and anchoring units, which are clustered by the self-association of pericentrin and assembled into larger structures by dynein-based transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Microtubule-nucleating and anchoring units are clustered by the self-association of pericentrin.
source: Taken together, our data show that pericentrin and γ-tubulin form microtubule-nucleating and anchoring units, which are clustered by the self-association of pericentrin and assembled into larger structures by dynein-based transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Microtubule-nucleating and anchoring units are assembled into larger structures by dynein-based transport.
source: Taken together, our data show that pericentrin and γ-tubulin form microtubule-nucleating and anchoring units, which are clustered by the self-association of pericentrin and assembled into larger structures by dynein-based transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: CDK5RAP2 contributes to microtubule nucleation efficiency.
source: CDK5RAP2 contributes to microtubule nucleation efficiency, whereas ninein appears to act somewhat later and contributes to the formation of a compact PCM cluster and a radial microtubule network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Ninein appears to act somewhat later and contributes to the formation of a compact PCM cluster and a radial microtubule network.
source: CDK5RAP2 contributes to microtubule nucleation efficiency, whereas ninein appears to act somewhat later and contributes to the formation of a compact PCM cluster and a radial microtubule network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: All these proteins (pericentrin, γ-tubulin, CDK5RAP2, ninein) can cluster in the absence of centrioles, and together they can efficiently nucleate and anchor microtubules.
source: Importantly, all these proteins can cluster in the absence of centrioles, and together they can efficiently nucleate and anchor microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In centrinone-treated wild-type cells, CAMSAP2-bound microtubule minus ends were anchored at the Golgi.
source: In centrinone-treated wild-type cells, CAMSAP2-bound microtubule minus ends were anchored at the Golgi (Wu et al., 2016; Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and a citation.

claim: In centrinone-treated AKAP450 knockout cells, CAMSAP2-bound microtubule minus ends were distributed randomly.
source: whereas in centrinone-treated AKAP450 knockout cells they were distributed randomly (Figures 1D and 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 6A.

claim: CAMSAP2-decorated minus ends displayed only limited motility on the scale of hours and thus formed a relatively stationary, disorganized microtubule network.
source: Live imaging showed that CAMSAP2-decorated minus ends displayed only limited motility on the scale of hours and thus formed a relatively stationary, disorganized microtubule network (Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging shown in Video 4.

claim: In centrinone-treated AKAP450 knockout cells, small PCM clusters were distributed throughout the cytoplasm.
source: Live imaging of GFP-CDK5RAP2 together with SiR-tubulin in these cells demonstrated that small PCM clusters were distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Small PCM clusters in centrinone-treated AKAP450 knockout cells moved along microtubules and encountered each other, but the direction of the movements was random and the clusters did not coalesce into a single structure.
source: These clusters moved along microtubules and encountered each other, but the direction of the movements was random and the clusters did not coalesce into a single structure (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging shown in Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, and Video 5.

claim: Treatment with dynapyrazole A strongly inhibited the movements of small PCM clusters in centrinone-treated AKAP450 knockout cells.
source: Treatment with dynapyrazole A strongly inhibited the movements of small PCM clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E, Video 6), indicating that they are dynein-driven.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E, and Video 6.

claim: The movements of small PCM clusters in centrinone-treated AKAP450 knockout cells are dynein-driven.
source: Treatment with dynapyrazole A strongly inhibited the movements of small PCM clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E, Video 6), indicating that they are dynein-driven.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dynapyrazole A treatment data.

claim: After the depletion of pericentrin in AKAP450 knockout cells, GFP-CDK5RAP2 became completely diffuse, and it failed to form clusters during nocodazole treatment or washout.
source: After the depletion of pericentrin, GFP-CDK5RAP2 became completely diffuse, and it failed to form clusters during nocodazole treatment or washout (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Video 7), indicating that clustering of GFP-CDK5RAP2 in AKAP450 knockout cells is pericentrin-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Video 7.

claim: Clustering of GFP-CDK5RAP2 in AKAP450 knockout cells is pericentrin-dependent.
source: After the depletion of pericentrin, GFP-CDK5RAP2 became completely diffuse, and it failed to form clusters during nocodazole treatment or washout (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Video 7), indicating that clustering of GFP-CDK5RAP2 in AKAP450 knockout cells is pericentrin-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pericentrin depletion data.

claim: In AKAP450 knockout cells, pericentrin still forms PCM clusters that can nucleate microtubules and can be moved by dynein along other microtubules.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that in AKAP450 knockout cells, pericentrin still forms PCM clusters that can nucleate microtubules and can be moved by dynein along other microtubules, similar to what occurs in wild-type cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In the absence of AKAP450, CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubules form a disorganized network, which imposes a random motility pattern on pericentrin-dependent PCM clusters and thus prevents their assembly into a single caMTOC.
source: However, in the absence of AKAP450, CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubules form a disorganized network, which imposes a random motility pattern on pericentrin-dependent PCM clusters and thus prevents their assembly into a single caMTOC, likely because PCM interactions are not sufficient to trigger their stable association (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Upon heterodimerizer addition in cells expressing FKBP-linked CAMSAP2 and FRB-linked ppKin14, ppKin14 was rapidly recruited to CAMSAP2-decorated microtubule ends.
source: However, upon heterodimerizer addition, ppKin14 was rapidly recruited to CAMSAP2-decorated microtubule ends, and after 2 hr, more than 90% of cells acquired a radial microtubule organization (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: After 2 hr of heterodimerizer treatment, more than 90% of cells expressing FKBP-linked CAMSAP2 and FRB-linked ppKin14 acquired a radial microtubule organization.
source: However, upon heterodimerizer addition, ppKin14 was rapidly recruited to CAMSAP2-decorated microtubule ends, and after 2 hr, more than 90% of cells acquired a radial microtubule organization (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: In heterodimerizer-treated cells expressing FKBP-linked CAMSAP2 and FRB-linked ppKin14, CAMSAP2-bound microtubule minus ends formed either a tight cluster or a 'whirlpool-like' ring in the cell center.
source: In heterodimerizer-treated cells, CAMSAP2-bound microtubule minus ends formed either a tight cluster or a 'whirlpool-like' ring in the cell center (Figure 6D–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The major caMTOC components, pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin, and ninein were concentrated within the CAMSAP2 cluster in heterodimerizer-treated cells.
source: The major caMTOC components, pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin, and ninein were also concentrated within the CAMSAP2 cluster (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The positioning of stabilized minus-ends is an important determinant of the overall microtubule organization and PCM localization in interphase cells.
source: These data indicate that the positioning of stabilized minus-ends is an important determinant of the overall microtubule organization and PCM localization in interphase cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the heterodimerization experiments.

claim: After heterodimerizer addition in centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells expressing FKBP-linked CAMSAP2 and FRB-linked ppKin14, microtubules acquired a radial organization.
source: After heterodimerizer addition, microtubules in cells expressing both constructs acquired a radial organization, but their minus ends usually did not converge in a single spot but rather accumulated in a~30–70 µm-large ring-like structure (Figure 7A and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and Video 8.

claim: In centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells after heterodimerizer addition, microtubule minus ends usually did not converge in a single spot but rather accumulated in a~30–70 µm-large ring-like structure.
source: After heterodimerizer addition, microtubules in cells expressing both constructs acquired a radial organization, but their minus ends usually did not converge in a single spot but rather accumulated in a~30–70 µm-large ring-like structure (Figure 7A and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and Video 8.

claim: In heterodimerizer-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells, CDK5RAP2 and γ-tubulin were enriched in the vicinity of CAMSAP2-positive microtubule minus ends, whereas ninein appeared rather diffuse.
source: Staining for PCM markers showed that CDK5RAP2 and γ-tubulin were enriched in the vicinity of CAMSAP2-positive microtubule minus ends, whereas ninein appeared rather diffuse (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In heterodimerizer-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells, the majority of mitochondria were found within the CAMSAP2 ring.
source: To determine the nature of the structure 'corralled' by the ring of CAMSAP2-decorated minus ends in heterodimerizer -treated cells, we stained for different membrane organelles and found that although there was no strong correlation with the nucleus, Golgi membranes, or lysosomes, the majority of mitochondria were found within the CAMSAP2 ring, and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) displayed increased density overlapping with the CAMSAP2 ring (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In heterodimerizer-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) displayed increased density overlapping with the CAMSAP2 ring.
source: To determine the nature of the structure 'corralled' by the ring of CAMSAP2-decorated minus ends in heterodimerizer -treated cells, we stained for different membrane organelles and found that although there was no strong correlation with the nucleus, Golgi membranes, or lysosomes, the majority of mitochondria were found within the CAMSAP2 ring, and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) displayed increased density overlapping with the CAMSAP2 ring (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In the absence of pericentrin, CAMSAP2-decorated minus ends were brought together by ppKin14, but their convergence was inefficient and possibly impeded by membrane organelles enriched in the central, thicker part of the cell.
source: It therefore appeared that in the absence of pericentrin, CAMSAP2-decorated minus ends were brought together by ppKin14, but their convergence was inefficient and possibly impeded by membrane organelles enriched in the central, thicker part of the cell before heterodimerizer addition (see the upper panel of Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Transient transfection of centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells with GFP-pericentrin rescued the formation of a tight CAMSAP2 cluster upon heterodimerizer treatment.
source: Transient transfection of centrinone-treated AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells with GFP-pericentrin rescued the formation of a tight CAMSAP2 cluster upon heterodimerizer treatment (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Pericentrin-containing PCM contributes to the formation of a caMTOC driven by minus-end-directed transport of CAMSAP2-stabilized minus-ends.
source: Our data show that pericentrin-containing PCM contributes to the formation of a caMTOC driven by minus-end-directed transport of CAMSAP2-stabilized minus-ends.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Coupling stable minus-ends to a minus-end directed motor is by itself insufficient to form a compact MTOC.
source: Importantly, our experiments and simulations showed that coupling stable minus-ends to a minus-end directed motor is by itself insufficient to form a compact MTOC, but self-clustering PCM can contribute to this process, when the clusters of PCM proteins that can anchor microtubules are sufficiently abundant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and simulations.

claim: Self-clustering PCM can contribute to the formation of a compact MTOC, when the clusters of PCM proteins that can anchor microtubules are sufficiently abundant.
source: Importantly, our experiments and simulations showed that coupling stable minus-ends to a minus-end directed motor is by itself insufficient to form a compact MTOC, but self-clustering PCM can contribute to this process, when the clusters of PCM proteins that can anchor microtubules are sufficiently abundant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and simulations.

claim: Self-association of interphase PCM appears to be strong enough to promote its clustering but is sufficiently dynamic to allow PCM reorganization dependent on other microtubule regulators present in the cell.
source: Altogether, self-association of interphase PCM appears to be strong enough to promote its clustering but is sufficiently dynamic to allow PCM reorganization dependent on other microtubule regulators present in the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Simulations of 300 PCM complexes reproducibly reached a steady state in which they formed a compact centrally located cluster.
source: First, we sought to recapitulate the formation of a single PCM cluster. Simulations of 300 of such PCM complexes reproducibly reached a steady state in which they formed a compact centrally located cluster (Figure 8A, Video 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 8A and Video 9A.

claim: If adhesive interactions between PCM complexes were disabled in simulations, they formed a loose ring-like arrangement and not a compact cluster.
source: However, if we disabled the adhesive interactions between PCM complexes, they formed a loose ring-like arrangement and not a compact cluster (Figure 8B, Video 9B)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 8B and Video 9B.

claim: Approximately 150 PCM complexes were needed to observe robust clustering in simulations.
source: Systematic variation of the number of PCM complexes in the system indicated that approximately 150 PCM complexes were needed to observe robust clustering (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Simulations support the idea that PCM components form a central cluster through positive feedback of dynein molecules carrying them toward the minus ends of microtubules attached to other PCM proteins.
source: Taken together, our simulations support the idea that PCM components form a central cluster through positive feedback of dynein molecules carrying them toward the minus ends of microtubules attached to other PCM proteins, and that adhesive interactions between the PCM complexes promote cluster compaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation data.

claim: Adhesive interactions between the PCM complexes promote cluster compaction in simulations.
source: Taken together, our simulations support the idea that PCM components form a central cluster through positive feedback of dynein molecules carrying them toward the minus ends of microtubules attached to other PCM proteins, and that adhesive interactions between the PCM complexes promote cluster compaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation data.

claim: For PCM self-organization to emerge in simulations, a sufficient number of PCM complexes must be present in the system.
source: For such self-organization to emerge, a sufficient number of PCM complexes must be present in the system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation data.

claim: In simulations with 300 microtubules growing from randomly distributed stationary CAMSAP2-stabilized ends and only 50 of 300 PCM complexes nucleating microtubules, the PCM cluster formation was disrupted.
